cells.tense: Something's arriving and you're at the door, pen already in hand.
cells.ask: Offer up one thing that's ending now and say plainly why it's done — one honest sentence to one person who can hear it, no apology, no footnote. It hands you back a clear line you can stand behind.
cells.core:
Endings land well for you lately, and you're not white-knuckling them. Something finishes and you let it finish; something shows up and you pick it up without second-guessing the timing. It isn't that you don't care what closes — it's that you know what's done and what's ready, and you act like it. People around you feel that steadiness even when they can't name it.

The piece free to grow now is fairness that isn't worked out on paper. Not scorekeeping, not making the split exact — just what's right, answered without reaching for the calculator. You're in a flowing exchange already; the question is whether you keep it flowing when the next thing arrives and the proportions look uneven for a stretch.
cells.sheetLine: You let things end fully, and you take what arrives as it comes.
cells.verb: letting what is finished actually finish, so the next thing has room to arrive
cells.place: the threshold where something from outside is starting to have weight

cells.tense: The shove hasn't come, but you're already braced for it, living a few steps into a future nobody's written.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're about to cut loose and, before you touch it, say out loud one sentence on what it would take to genuinely complete — no follow-up, no trashing. It gives you back a real comparison in place of a reflex.
cells.core:
You're clearing things before they've been lived — projects, ties, arrangements — and the clearing feels like freedom while it runs. From the outside it looks decisive. From the inside it's mostly speed. The next thing rarely gets longer than the last one did, because ending it early keeps you ahead of a shove that hasn't arrived.

The way back lies through someone else's actual face. Sitting with one other person, listening to what they think is happening — including the part where they disagree — would slow you down enough that the timing stops being yours to force. What that offers: staying you while feeling what they feel. The hard part is that some endings you've performed would turn out to have been rehearsals, and that's a thing to sit with.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending things early and calling it freedom.
cells.verb: letting what is finished actually finish, so the next thing has room to arrive
cells.place: the threshold where something from outside is starting to have weight

cells.tense: A door closed behind you and you're still standing there watching it like it might open.
cells.ask: Name one thing that already ended — out loud, one sentence, the date it actually ended if you can find it — then go do one concrete errand for the life that's next. The sentence is the door closing; the errand is your hand on the next handle.
cells.core:
Nothing's moving because nothing's been allowed to finish. You keep the thing that's already done sitting at the table, loyal to it in a way that takes something from every morning — and the new thing trying to arrive keeps finding no room. Waiting for a sign, or a permission, or one more week doesn't open it; the room only opens when the old thing is actually done.

The charge comes around sideways, through motion rather than mourning. Moving on something you genuinely want, done from the feeling you're already carrying, loosens the grip the past has on the present. It pulls the current through the place where things arrive. Setting it down means saying a thing is over to someone who was in it with you, and that part won't be quiet.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping something alive that's already finished.
cells.verb: letting what is finished actually finish, so the next thing has room to arrive

cells.tense: Something is going in you and you haven't put it into words, not even for yourself.
cells.ask: Write one sentence naming what's already over, in your own words, and put it somewhere you'll see it tomorrow — a note, a photo, a message to yourself. That's it. The sentence hands you back the steering you've been letting drift stand in for.
cells.core:
You've been saying the drift is just what's happening — nothing in particular, no reason — but you've been changing your life anyway. Dropping things, not re-upping, letting certain threads go quiet. What you haven't done is mark that you're the one doing it. The arranging is already yours; the saying-so isn't.

The way back goes through plain structure — writing something down, saying what's already decided somewhere it can be read. That's what gives things shape, and it's what people feel in your presence when it's working. Once it's written down, it stops being something that just happens to you. What that could give: things start making sense again, in your own handwriting.

attempts.check: The draft's weakest claim is that a reader can name what is dying in someone before the person has said anything — the record only supports that the ending is unowned, not that a specific thing is going. A reader might fairly say the opposite: that they ended something recently and felt nothing much either way, or that the word 'chosen' flatters them. The asks survive being wrong because each one produces an artifact — a sentence in their own voice, a hypothetical with a punchline, a date said out loud — that teaches them something whether or not the reading fits. The sentence that serves the writer is the closing clause about repair and thanks; it is pretty and it does not tell the person what to do next, so it has to earn its place or go.
